name: Campbell's Law
statement: The more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to monitor.
statementAccent: the more subject it will be to corruption pressures
meaning: The harder a society leans on one number to make its decisions, the more that number gets gamed — and the more the activity behind it bends out of shape to feed it.
example: A school district ties funding and job security to a single reading test. Test scores climb every year, while the library period is cut to make room for test drill and pupils who would drag the average down are quietly reclassified out of the tested group. The score goes up; reading does not.
whyItMatters: This is the sharper, more institutional cousin of Goodhart's Law: it predicts not just a bad metric but real damage to the thing being measured. Wherever a single indicator carries high stakes — test scores, crime statistics, hospital waiting times — expect both the gaming and the collateral distortion, and design the stakes accordingly.
origin: The social psychologist Donald T. Campbell set it out in "Assessing the Impact of Planned Social Change", where he introduced it as one of two "pessimistic laws". The paper had a tangled publication history that citations often garble: a version was presented at a conference in Visegrád, Hungary in May 1974; it was published in 1975 as a chapter in Gene M. Lyons's Social Research and Public Policies (Public Affairs Center, Dartmouth College); it was reprinted in December 1976, with Dartmouth's permission, as Paper #8 in the Occasional Paper Series of the Evaluation Center at Western Michigan University; and it reached its widest audience when Evaluation and Program Planning ran it in 1979.
